messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ava had always been drawn to hands-on work, and her job as an electrician gave her a sense of satisfaction that few other things could. But since the car accident six months ago, even the simplest tasks seemed to hold a hidden threat. It wasn't just the physical danger that came with working at heights or around live wires – it was the constant feeling of unease that had settled in her bones. Talking about the future, which used to be something she loved doing with friends and family, now made her skin crawl. Whenever someone asked her what she wanted to do next year, or five years from now, Ava felt a familiar knot form in her stomach. She couldn't shake the thought that she might not even make it that far – that some other accident, some other cruel twist of fate, could be waiting just around the corner. It was as if the crash had shown her how fragile life really was, and now every plan seemed like a reckless gamble. When driving with others, Ava couldn't help but replay the moments leading up to the collision in her mind. The memories were hazy, but she remembered feeling trapped, unable to move or escape as the other car bore down on them. Now, whenever someone else was behind the wheel, she felt that same sense of powerlessness wash over her. Cars hit by accident – even just seeing them on the side of the road – made her heart skip a beat, and for a moment, it would all come flooding back. As Ava struggled to make sense of these fears, she began to doubt herself more and more. She couldn't trust that she'd do the right thing in an emergency; what if she froze up like she had during the accident? What if her instincts were wrong, and she made things worse instead of better? This self-doubt crept into every area of her life, making it hard for Ava to feel confident about anything. The injustice of what happened still simmered just below the surface. Nothing had been done about the other driver – no charges filed, no consequences at all. It felt like a slap in the face, a reminder that some people could get away with almost anything and leave others to pick up the pieces. This sense of powerlessness further eroded Ava's faith in herself; if the world wasn't just or fair, how could she trust her own judgment? As time went on, even Ava's body began to feel unreliable. Some days, her muscles ached as if she'd been running for miles, while others left her feeling weak and lethargic. She couldn't shake the fear that there was still something wrong inside her, something that the doctors had missed or overlooked. This nagging uncertainty only added to her growing list of fears. As Ava's friends and family tried to reassure her, she found herself pulling away from them. Talking about the future seemed like a cruel joke; what was the point when anything could happen at any moment? Driving with others made her anxious, and even thinking about it triggered those same old memories and fears. Her loved ones didn't understand why Ava couldn't just "move on" or "get over it," but to her, the danger felt very real indeed. It wasn't until Ava found herself turning down job after job because they involved driving with others that she realized how much these fears had taken over her life. She was stuck in a cycle of avoidance and self-doubt, unable to shake the memories of that terrible day. It was then that Ava finally decided to seek help – not just for her own sake, but for the sake of those around her who were tired of watching her live in fear. Ava's greatest hope now is that she can learn to trust herself and her body again, to quiet the doubts that plague her every waking moment. But as she looks ahead to the uncertain future, one thing remains clear: the memories of that crash will always be there, waiting to ambush her at any turn.
